Revised when results or the idea change.)

## 1. The story in one paragraph
Practitioners search prompts/pipelines on a benchmark's items and report the best configuration's score on those same items. That number is the maximum of K noisy estimates, so it can overstate how the deployed configuration performs on fresh items; whether it does, by how much, and whether conclusions drawn from such numbers (tuned beats untuned, tool A beats tool B) survive, is an empirical question — selection-bias and post-selection-inference theory exists (e.g. Cawley–Talbot; Rink–Brannath for same-sample simultaneous bounds), and meta-analyses of leaderboards find little adaptive overfitting. We answer it with a **ground-truth measurement** on a real LLM and MMLU-Pro (cached item × configuration matrix, rotated verification on disjoint fresh items, uncertainty from disjoint search sets and a pool bootstrap), explain the size by quantities visible in the search log (n, effective number of competing configurations K_eff, spread of true quality σ_θ), carry the drivers to regimes the real matrix cannot reach with a **validated** semi-synthetic arm, and compare **reporting protocols at equal item budget**. The **candidate protocol** is a max-t simultaneous lower bound computed from the logged item-level score matrix over a declared candidate set; split-report and nested CV are the controls it must match or beat on the criteria of §2.1; its failure regimes (adaptive/nested-subset search) are mapped. The paper also gives a practitioner recipe, *what to log and report* (§4, Box 1). If the candidate fails, the paper says so and recommends the control that does best. A push to your repository's `main`, or to `dev` of `paper-repo` (below), is a delivery; a local commit is not. A file over 20 MiB, and data files in bulk whatever their size (`*.npz`, `*.csv` and the like), go in Git LFS (`git lfs track '<pattern>'` before adding them).
